Make a reversible, registered comparison of the two cards. Transparency and matching marks justify this experiment; they do not establish what it will reveal.

First label the copies A/B, their original faces, and the dotted corners. Match all four registration marks, preserving their order. There is a geometric distinction worth checking: matching opposite edges by translation places equal rectangles alongside each other, whereas flipping one copy left-to-right can bring those edges together with the cards overlapping. A half-turn also exchanges left and right but reverses vertical order. Try the configurations compatible with the actual mark pattern; do not force a fit by stretching or adjusting individual strokes. Record where the corner dots land and how asymmetric strokes change. They can distinguish orientations that otherwise look similar, although coincident dots are not an established requirement.

Inspect both seam continuity in the adjoining arrangement and complementary strokes in a registered overlay. Use differently colored tracings if necessary to distinguish three views: all strokes together, strokes shared by both cards, and strokes present in exactly one. The title makes the shared-versus-different comparison worth trying; it does not uniquely specify exclusive-or.

The learning goal is to discover whether one simple placement produces repeated, coherent completions or a systematic distinction between shared and unique marks. One accidental letter-like patch would be weak evidence. If a pattern emerges, freeze the placement and comparison rule, then inspect the rest of the strokes and competing placements without local exceptions. A broad, consistent result would support that version; failure would redirect attention to another permitted orientation or the seam. No overlay has been inspected here, so there is no observed message yet.

The description strongly suggests the eight trigrams, or bagua, associated with the I Ching: three continuous/broken lines give exactly eight patterns. That identifies a promising notation family, not its role on this page.

The useful next step is a faithful transcription preserving pair order, line order, compass orientation, and every arrow's endpoints. Record each trigram provisionally as three bits, top-to-bottom, with continuous = 1 and broken = 0. This is an explicit recording convention, not a claim about traditional reading order. The smallest useful reference would be an accurate trigram/hexagram table covering line-order conventions and the Earlier Heaven and Later Heaven directional arrangements; no lookup has been performed here.

Develop two interpretations:

1. Paired trigrams form hexagrams. Stack each pair into six lines under one fixed assignment of first/second to lower/upper. Pair order alone does not tell us which assignment is intended. Compare arrow-linked six-line patterns: do arrows mark a reproducible transformation, such as a line change or exchange of halves? An observed pattern would generate a rule to check on the remaining arrows. Hexagram names or numbers may become useful after the stacking convention is justified; they do not automatically yield letters.

2. Trigrams supply compass positions. The compass makes a directional arrangement worth checking. Use a documented arrangement with a fixed orientation, retaining both common arrangements if nothing selects one. Represent each ordered pair as a directed connection between its two positions. Check whether the printed links consistently connect the end of one pair to the beginning of another, or impose another reproducible spatial relation. Do not choose rotations, layouts, and arrow meanings separately for each pair.

Both interpretations explain pairing differently. Actual pair identities and arrow structure are needed to compare their consequences. A generic three-bit encoding remains possible, but freely converting pairs into alphabet indices would leave the compass and arrows unexplained. Symbol recognition is useful progress; neither the directional interpretation nor a final decoding is established.

The current word establishes only that one selected combination of labels, order, and shifts produces a plausible word. The synonym substitutions and broad search make it a weak candidate, not a checked solution. Preserve its exact derivation, but stop tuning it toward the same output.

Investigate the features the extraction ignored: the empty location and the five altered states. Obtain a coordinate-preserving transcription of all 25 cells, with natural object labels kept alongside alternatives, and describe each altered object's orientation or condition separately from its name. The blank's coordinates and the five abnormal cells' coordinates and precise states are the most urgent missing inputs.

Three clue-grounded possibilities deserve bounded checks:

• Movement: the blank may be an origin or vacancy, and unusual states may indicate directions or moves. Check whether the abnormal cells and their visible orientations define a coherent route involving the blank. If considering sliding, explicitly restrict the trial to an adjacent tile entering the blank and track the changing vacancy. A 5-by-5 board with one blank suggests a sliding-puzzle representation, but supplies neither legal moves nor a target by itself. Do not invent them to make a route work.

• Operations or rebuses: the altered condition may do work. Describe states without reference to the desired word, then test whether a consistent relationship turns ordinary names or shapes into new units. For example, a reversed object could motivate testing reversal, but a sideways cup does not by itself prescribe reversing CUP. Require a common explanatory rule or clearly indicated operation set; keep unresolved names unresolved. The blank might denote a missing item or SPACE only if the same reading supports that role.

• Selection and coordinates: five unusual objects may select five cells. Check whether they occupy one per row or column, or another conspicuous arrangement, before choosing an order. A coordinate extraction would additionally need an evidenced key; the grid size alone does not establish a Polybius square.

Choose between these by geometry and state descriptions before reading off letters: adjacency and consistent directions favor movement; repeatable state-to-operation relationships favor rebuses; systematic positions plus a key favor coordinate extraction. Account for ordinary cells as well, without assuming every one must yield a letter.

Previously seen labels cannot become a blind holdout by setting some aside now. They can still constrain a revised rule retrospectively. With no image or oracle, these checks remain proposed; the concrete next step is to acquire the missing spatial/state transcription.
